Xian wrote:
[Dracula, blood, sex?]
> You are free to remain unimpressed. Read it as a straight horror
> novel, if you like. I find it hard to deny that sexual undercurrents
> run through the book.

I did not realize we were debating whether _Dracula_ contained "sexual
undercurrents" (whatever that means). I thought we were debating
whether the vampire's drinking of blood represented sex, or whether
Stoker concieved his vampire as erotic and sexy.

> All of the female characters
>had some sort of
> infatuation or liasons with the Count,

By "all" you mean "both", I suppose.
The count also has sex with Reinfield, with Harker, and
with an entire shipload of sailors, assuming, of course, that
drinking blood represents sex. I also seem to recall that
Lucy has sex with an infant. These deep insights sure are
enlightening.

As for "infatuation", the count also used his mind-control
powers on Reinfield as well. It was necessary for the author
to explain the count's "appeal" in supernatural terms, because,
after all, the count was not *in fact* the least appealing. He
was an undead, devouring, corpse-creature (presumably
incapable of sex) and any "appeal" he posessed was an
illusion (surely I have already addressed this point).

> in various states of undress

By this I suppose you mean that they were wearing their
nightclothes when the count attacked them at night.
But whatever. If he did portray them in "varying states
of undress" (which I do not recall) this would imply to me
an erotic interest on the part of the male author in his attractive
female characters (and not in the undead male corpse-creature).

You need to refocus yourself on the count and argue the sexual
significance of his specifically *vampiric* qualities. At present,
you are casting your net awfully wide in search of material
to support your argument, which is a universal practice among
"neo-Freudian" literary critics. Inevitably, such attempts succeed
because all humans have sex organs and sex instincts, and therefore
everything human can be connected to sex by playing loose
games of association. The "insights" that result are useless.
Anything can be related to sex by playing loose association games,
including your rolled-up dirty socks..

>or intimacy.

I guess by this you mean that he got close enough to drink
their blood.

> Do you take all fiction at face value and not look for any hidden or
> deeper meanings?

LOL. You talk about "deeper meanings" in connection with the
notion that drinking blood represents sex in Dracula. Yet applying
this metaphor quickly turns the story into incomprehensible
nonsense. A "straight" (ie. non-allegorical) reading of the story
is a thousand times more "deep" than the nonsensical porno-allegory
that such a theory produces.

A lot of interesting (*) things might be said about the significance
and real-life applicability of the vampire myth, both in folklore
and as portrayed in Stoker's novel. One may note, for instance,
the significance of the vampire as a personification of disease,
contagion, and lingering death. Garlic, an extremely nutritious herb
known to boost the immune system, is said to be proof against them.
If another sort of real-life applicability is desired, one may compare
the relationship between a vampire and his victim to various real-life
relationships between men and women, in which one partner is so
arrested and infantile in his/her emotional development, and so
emotionally needy, that he/she ends up emotionally devouring,
and ultimately destroying, his or her partner. In real life, such
relationships are often (on the surface) romantic or sexual.(**)
But it is not the SEX that is analagous to blood drain .... not at
any rate if the analogy is to make sense.

(*) Interesting, at least, to those who are interested in other things
besides sex.

(**) Similarly, in Stoker's novel, the count seems to have a preference
for victims of the opposite gender, and disguises his depredations,
(to an minimal extent) as romantic courtship. But to argue, therefore, that
vampirism represents sexuality is to rather miss the point. This is
merely a ruse and an illusion that covers a hidden horror. Any lure
of sex & romance is a false promise ... something the
vampire has no intention (or capability) of actually providing. It is a bait
and switch. Therein lies the horror.

It is important to recall that "Dracula" is definitely intended to be a
*horror*
story, and that its vampires were intended to be *horrible.* People who
try to equate Stoker's vampires with sexuality base this on the
idea that Stoker and his contemporaries were so sexually repressed that they
regarded sex as horrible. But this seems to me very unlikely. While they
were certainly more reserved about discussing it openly, I am reasonably
sure that most Victorians thought that sex was great, much as we do now.

> Did you read Frankenstein as a pure horror story?

I believe my phrase (with reference to "Dracula") was "straight horror
story", by which I mean to say it is not an allegory (sexual or otherwise).
I did not use the phrase "pure horror story", nor do I have any idea
what you intend the phrase to mean..

And no, I don't think "Frankenstein" is an allegory either, and
certainly not a sexual one. (In other words, it is a "straight horror
story"). It has a moral and a message, of course, and Shelly is
pretty up-front about it (it is pretty much announced in the subtitle)..

(BTW, in case anyone has not read it, Shelly kicks Stoker's ass in
the horror department. No film version yet made has done her novel,
or her monster, justice.)

> The Jungle is just something about a guy in a meat factory?

May well be for all I know. I never read it. Does the "meat" represent sex?

> 1984...just another sordid, tawdry romance in a futuristic police
>state?

Getting carried away, aren't you? Why do you imagine I possess such
an opinion? That is certainly not the one-line review I would give for
"1984". However, it is certainly not a sexual allegory. If it were, that
would probably cheapen it, and make it sordid and tawdry.

<snip more straw-man literary opinions you falsely imagine I possess>

>> > I did not say that the entirety of the vampire myth is about sex...
>>
>> No, you merely suggested that my interest and preference for
non-erotic
>> vampires was somehow unreasonable and contradictory. I believe my
response was
>> appropriate.

> Actually, I didn't say that it's unreasonable. I said that current
> fiction likes to portray them as erotic,

Which was something I had just said when you intervened
with your comment. I'm sorry. I did not realize you were merely
trying to agree with me.

> and I'm not making a
> judgement on that one way or another. I tend to agree that the
> vampire is over-hyped as an erotic symbol, and I don't believe I said
> anything about you being wrong for not agreeing with the current trend
> in pop culture.

So you were just trying to agree with me all along. Shucks!

{re: idea that drinking blood represents sex in Dracula]
> Go right ahead...it was obviously dreamed up by some idiot in an ivory
> tower who knows nothing about the subject.

Now yer catchin on!

> > Well that makes two of us. Nonetheless, I derived considerable
enjoyment from
> > "Dracula", even though I did not find the title character even
remotely sexy.
> > How about you? I read it as a straight horror story. I strongly
suspect that
> > this is precisely what Bram Stoker intended, whatever the "standard
> > interpretation" might be.

> Actually, I don't think that's what he intended. I think he intended
> elements of horror in the novel in order to bypass censors, and to
> keep it titillating for his Victorian readers,

Hmm. This statement is a bit nebulous. By denying that he intended it
as "straight horror" do you mean that he intended it as sexual allegory?
Do you think he really desired to write soft-core porn, but was forced
disguised it as horror? Why else would he wish to get anything past
the censors? If soft-core porn or erotic drama were his real interest, then
how come he knew so much about folklore?

Francis Ford Coppola seems to have bought into ideas such as these.
In his so-called "Bram Stoker's Dracula", he insists on taking the count
seriously as a romantic and erotic hero. He makes the alleged
hidden eroticism of the novel quite explicit, presumably on the assumption
that this is what Stoker would have wanted had not those mean
Victorian censors stopped him. The resulting film is a bit of a joke,
not scary, and impossible to take seriously as horror -- arguably one of
the least successful adaptations of the novel. Particularly
funny is the scene where a "horrified" Harker is fed upon by Dracula's
brides, there portrayed as a trio of luscious bare-breasted beauties
caressing him on satin sheets. Thank God he was able to escape!

> but it's also not that
> much of a leap (for me, at least) to read hidden desires in the
> actions of the characters.

You are once again being extremely nebulous here. Which characters
are you refering to? What hidden desires? Let me remind you once again
that we were originally debating your explicit claim that, in Dracula, the act
of
drinking blood is a metaphorical representation of sex. Suggesting
that certain unnamed characters may have hidden desires of a sexual
nature, somewhere in the course of a full-length novel, does not sound like
it has much to do with your original claim.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <20010818120049...@mb-mm.news.cs.com>, MSheafer33
<mshea...@cs.com> writes

>James Coupe wrote:
>
>>Erm, drawing links with sex doesn't necessarily turn something into a
>>"nonsensical porno-allegory".
>
>Not necessarily, but we were discussing a particular situation.

And drawing links between vampirism, vampiric feeding and sex does not
turn the book into a "nonsensical porno-allegory" either. Allegory is a
useful thing to consider at all points, of course.

>We were
>discussing the theory that in Dracula, drinking blood is a metaphorical
>representation of sex. That is closer to equating than it is to relating.

Indeed, many things can be metaphoric. One of the useful things about
metaphors is that they allow you to compare and contrast the
similarities and differences between two items, delineating knowledge
and improving insight into both items at the same time.

Metaphors do not, however, immediately make one thing the other. There
is only so far that a metaphor can be taken. One element of criticism
and interpretation is recognising how far these metaphors can be taken,
and on what levels - figurative, literal, psychological, sociological
etc.

>> Just in case anyone was wondering.
>>Literary interpretation and symbolism are a little more intricate than
>>that.
>
>OK. You are more than welcome, if you can, to explain how this particular
>theory improves one's understanding and appreciation of the story.

Why would you have literary interpretation solely address the story
aspect? It can be far more enriching and rewarding than just that.
Indeed, a well-written piece of literature can be, indeed some might say
*should* be, about far more than simply the story.

I can indeed write an essay for you on these uses of symbolism and
metaphor in Dracula. However, I have problems accessing a well-stocked
academic library, at present, for cross-referential and research
purposes.

I would suggest a web-search might prove valuable to you, presenting you
with many and varied options rather than sticking solely to one. One of
the key things with reading criticism is to never read only author or
point of view if you can possibly help it.

As another person's point of view, I'd suggest "Nosferatu" (the film) or
"Shadow of the Vampire" (also a film, set during the making of
Nosferatu) as particularly useful in this regard.

>>And the bisexual nature of the Count is one of the more pervasive and
>>persuasive readings of the novel that I've come across.
>
>This is presumably based on the fact that Dracula consumes the blood of both
>men and women.

Partly, but not just that. It's based on a lot more than that.

Literary interpretation and criticism is not a game of "This means that,
case solved." It may aid you in your argument to bear that in mind.
Literary criticism is a somewhat more delicate tool than that.

It may be possible to draw particular strands of imagery together for a
"This means that" interpretation when attempting a piece of Practical
Criticism or, to a lesser degree, when working with the whole piece
under the New Criticism - with such influences as IA Richards, Donald
Davie or FR Leavis brought to bear on the subject - but across a whole
novel, things become far more subtle, delicate and intricate.

I'd suggest Northrop Frye's "Anatomy of Criticism" as providing a few,
very useful, ways of interacting with a piece of literature. His work
has been criticised and, in some manners, surpassed by recent work (you
might find "The Language of Criticism" by Dr. John Casey (yes, this is a
real person, not a crypt card, I've met him) useful in this regard) but
it still provides a very useful base for literary criticism to work from
- a sort of "If I'm not thinking about these ideas, why?" point of
reference. The Frye is useful and generally available if you have
access to a well-stocked library.

>>Far from the
>>only reading, of course, what with subjectivism and deconstructionalism,
>>and all, but certainly a very valid and insightful interpretation.
>
>Hmm. This sounds like fence sitting to me. Do you support the theory or not?

Modern literary criticism and interpretation do not (necessarily)
require you to pick only one theory and support it (though this can be
useful if you're competing for funding, I guess). Unless a theory can
be written which illuminates each and every part of a well-written novel
(or poem, or play etc.), there's no harm in considering different
theories and view-points. Indeed, it's extremely useful - especially
when working with a deconstructionalist or subjective point of view.
The latter, especially considering the intensely subjective nature of
portions of the novel/experience, can be particularly illuminating and
liberating.

--
James Coupe PGP Key: 0x5D623D5D

Messages.Body:

Messages.Author: MSheafer33
Messages.Body:
James Coupe wrote:

>Indeed, many things can be metaphoric. One of the useful things about
>metaphors is that they allow you to compare and contrast the
>similarities and differences between two items, delineating knowledge
>and improving insight into both items at the same time.
>
>Metaphors do not, however, immediately make one thing the other. There
>is only so far that a metaphor can be taken. One element of criticism
>and interpretation is recognising how far these metaphors can be taken,
>and on what levels - figurative, literal, psychological, sociological
>etc.

These paragraphs suggest that we are speaking at cross purposes due to
different terminology. To my mind, the concept of a metaphor applies only one
thing directly represents another. Similes and comparisons do not a metaphor
make. When an element is said to "represent" sex, I take this as meaning
considerably more than saying that it can be related to sex or linked to sex,
or that connections can be drawn to sex. It is the former approach that I
dislike, as I feel that it has a tendency to oversimplify and reduce literature
to base elements by a failure to draw distinctions. While one thing can often
be related to another, and this can add to appreciation and understanding (if
the relationship is close enough to be meaningful), equating them can blur
distinctions and oversimplify.

>>OK. You are more than welcome, if you can, to explain how this particular
>>theory improves one's understanding and appreciation of the story.
>
>Why would you have literary interpretation solely address the story
>aspect? It can be far more enriching and rewarding than just that.
>Indeed, a well-written piece of literature can be, indeed some might say
>*should* be, about far more than simply the story.

Once again, we are at semantic cross purposes. To me, the concept of a story
encompasses everything in it. I do not think of "story" as a separate abstract
element of a work of fiction.

But rather than nitpick over words I would rather present a specific example
from Dracula (which is both the first erotic passage and the first bloodsucking
passage), and attempt to show why a metaphorical reading, with bloodsucking
representing sex, actually interferes with the appreciation of the passage.
Perhaps, even if you do not agree with me entirely, you will at least have some
idea where I am coming from. If all remain totally unimpressed, I will give up
and stop trying to explain myself, as my ideas are receiving little sympathy
overall, and I have no desire to keep hit my head against walls.

The passage occurs in Chapter 3, and involve Harkers first encounter with
Dracula's three "brides"or "children". While wandering in a forbidden part of
the castle, Harker falls asleep and wakes up to find 3 alluring but subtly
repulsive young women standing nearby. While Harker pretends to be asleep, the
three beauties talk in a manner that makes it sound like they wish to make
erotic love to him. "He is young and strong" they say. "There are kisses(*)
enough for us all." Harker, at this point, experiences a definite erotic
thrill, including an "agony of delightful anticipation," as one of the young
women approaches him. There can be no doubt as to the reason for Harker's
erotic thrill, as even a "repressed" Victorian can figure out what Harker
*thinks* these beauties have in mind.

[(*) "Kisses" is a metaphor, but, ironically, it is a reverse of the sort under
debate. Sex is being used as a metaphor for vampirism, rather than the other
way around. Similarly, with the terms "brides" and "children", normal human
relationships are used as metaphors for a unique vampiric one]

But to believe that bloodsucking is a metaphorical representation of sex, or to
otherwise believe that vampiric bloodsucking is erotically appealing, is, I
think, to miss out on the dark humour and irony of this situation.
Appreciation of this irony depends on keeping the concepts separate, and of
realizing that what Harker *thinks* they intend, and what they *actually*
intend are fundamentally different. Confounding the concepts detracts from the
mounting horror that results when both Harker and the reader realize that what
the ladies actually intend is SOMETHING ELSE.

And while this passage is undoubtedly erotic, it seems to me that the effect
that Stoker is trying to achieve here is primarily one of horror, rather than
titiliation. I find it comparable to the scene in The Shining, where Jack
Torrance is lured into the arms of what seems to be a beautiful naked woman,
only to discover that she is in fact SOMETHING ELSE. The eroticism and
titilation is significant primarily as an illusion, that leads to the shock of
realization and grotesque contrast. I think that the effect that Stoker was
attempting to achieve here can fairly be surmised from their context. The
opening 4 chapters -- arguably the best part of the book -- are justly famous
for their gradually mounting horror. I don't think this effect was achieved
accidentally. Stoker must have been fairly well focussed on producing just
that result.

So anyway the scene continues. The vampire presses lips, tongue, and fangs
against Harker's flesh, and, despite a subtly repulsive smell of blood on her
breath, the erotic illusion remains, as he waits in "langourous ecstasy" for
whatever she will do next. But before she can go further, the count
intervenes, and throws her off. Harker still pretends to sleep. He hears the
women demand that Dracula give them *something* to feed on, and, instead of
Harker, Dracula offers them a small child that he has just captured, and the
three vampire-women proceed to feed on the child instead. Both Harker and the
audience figure out what is going on at this point, and any illusions are
destroyed.

The erotic illusion is, in fact, shattered far more effectively than if the
women had actually fed on Harker. The first *actual* boodsucking portrayed in
the book involve these women devouring a small child. Not only is it difficult
to imagine anyone seeing this as erotically appealing; but the development
seems expressly calculated to destroy whatever appeal these women may have
seemed to possess. It reveals them as being the grotesque reverse of what a
woman's nature is supposed to be. They are not the type to nurture children;
they devour them instead. Rather than suckling children, they suck *on* them.
I suspect that most men would find this quite a turn-off, no matter how
physically attractive she might otherwise appear to be.

It certainly seems to have this effect on Harker, who is so horrified that he
passes out. While he was quite up-front in admitting their initial erotic
appeal for him, we hear no more such nonsense afterwards. We hear no more
poetic descriptions of their eyes and hair and skin. He merely says things
like "nothing can be more dreadful than those awful women" and "Faugh! Mina is
a woman and there is naught in common. They are demons of the Pit." Shortly
after making this latter statement, he attempts a near-suicidal climb to
freedom, because he figures no death can be more dreadful than one at their
hands.

Messages.Author: MSheafer33
Messages.Body:

>"donate blood" to her, inan attempt to bring that healthy look back to

Stoker, as i recall, has a quite a bit of fun with the idea that donation of

transferred blood to her.

>Again, I feel that, considering the prevailing morals of the time,

Messages.Author: MSheafer33
Messages.Body:
Xian wrote:

>> A lot of interesting (*) things might be said about the significance
>> and real-life applicability of the vampire myth, both in folklore
>> and as portrayed in Stoker's novel. One may note, for instance,
>> the significance of the vampire as a personification of disease,
>> contagion, and lingering death. Garlic, an extremely nutritious
>herb
>> known to boost the immune system, is said to be proof against them.
>
>Ah, but that's not a non-allegorical reading of it. You're turning
>the vampire into a symbol of disease, which quickly turns this into
>something other than a "straight" reading of the book.

You are confused as to the meaning of the term "allegory". In the story
Dracula (as in folklore) the vampire literally *is* a source of illness,
contagion, and lingering death. But he is also a person, and the story will
not be better understood if you ignore this fact. Therefore, a "straight
reading" is necessary. The associations made above merely present possible
relationships between the story and "real life". This can be done with all
stories, but all stories are not therefore allegories.

>> If another sort of real-life applicability is desired, one may
>compare
>> the relationship between a vampire and his victim to various
>real-life
>> relationships between men and women, in which one partner is so
>> arrested and infantile in his/her emotional development, and so
>> emotionally needy, that he/she ends up emotionally devouring,
>> and ultimately destroying, his or her partner. In real life, such
>> relationships are often (on the surface) romantic or sexual.(**)
>
>More allegory...you're turning this into a psycho-social reading of
>the book. Which certainly isn't a bad thing, but it's definitely not
>a "straight" readin

Nonsense. Dracula is a person. To suggest that he may have characteristics in
common with real people in real life, or that lessons drawn from his story can
be applied to similar but non-identical situations, has nothing to do with
making his story into an allegory.

It is merely a form of commentary, an attempt to find relevance and
relationships and applicability. It does not require us to pretend that
Dracula was intended to be anything other than he is literally presented as
being.

Messages.Author: MSheafer33
Messages.Body:
Cameron wrote:
[re Coppola's portrayal of Harker & the Vampire Ladies]

>That was accurate to their description in the book.

Really? In the book, they never actually feed upon him. And correct me if I'm
wrong, but I do not recall the devouring of the child being portrayed in the
film. I guess Coppola realized this would spoil the eroticism.

>Only through high
>morals and pure love for his girl was he able to escape the clutches
>of the ravenous beasts. Thank God indeed.

High morals and true love had little to do with it (in the book at least).
When he thought they were women, he seemed prepared to let them make love to
him, and escaped only because Dracula intervened. After that, he saw them
devour the child and figured out what they truly were. There was no more need
of high morals. He fled from them in a perfectly understandable state of
abject terror for his life.

Please see my analysis of this passage in my response to J. Coupe.

>As for the censors, yes he
>did need to get a bit around them.
>That didn't stop him from writing
>a good story though.

Agreed.

>In a deeper way though, the actual myths of
>Dracula place him in a similiar position of erotic monster. The movie
>was infact so "unsucessful" because it remained true to the plot of
>the book.

I disagree. While he may have been faithful in some details, Coppola missed to
boat when he assumed Stoker was going for titilation rather than horror. So he
enhances the eroticism, but fails to include the devouring of the child, which,
in Stoker's sequence, is the shock and horror that destroys the erotic
illusion.

>If you didn't see it as horror, then you've become to jaded
>to what Victorian horror is.

You have forgotten the devouring of the child AND of its mother, if you think
that a reasonably faithful adaptation (at least as faithful as Coppola's) could
not have been more horrifying than Coppola's..

> As a test, do you think that The Raven
>by Poe is scary?

Poe's "The Raven" was never scary. But it was (and is) horrifying (in a sort
of humorous way) in that it portrays psychological and existential dispair.

Sheafer, you're a shifty, shifty guy.

You've started arguing that drinking blood is clearly not intended to
be a sexual act, and that your complaint is with academics who
construct "Dracula" into a sexual allegory, but that's not what your
argument started out as. Back when this thread was about the sexual
content of the card Social Charm, Xian pointed out that the sexual
theme was perfectly in line with the sexual themes of the vampire myth
in general and with "Dracula" in particular:

Xian wrote:
> . . . The vampire myth (in its
> current, post-Victorian state) is all about eroticism, the act of
> drinking blood taking the place of sex, etc. . .

Your response was:

> . . . a number of
> interesting things (which I won't go into for now) could be said
> about the possible significance and applicability of the vampire
> myth, all of which are reduced to abject nonsense if you assume
> that the act of drinking blood represents sex. . . .

See the straw man?

Xian was talking about bloodsucking TAKING THE PLACE OF sex.

You pretended he was talking about bloodsucking REPRESENTING sex.

Obviously one of the horrors of the vampire myths is that the sex
act/drive is replaced with the hunger for blood. Stoker's Van Helsing
said as much, and as your own post about the three seductive vampires
in Dracula's castle would suggest, the main reason vampires would want
to have Social Charm would be to get into a position where they could
feed. Or Bleed.

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <20010819004726...@mb-fg.news.cs.com>, MSheafer33
<mshea...@cs.com> writes

>These paragraphs suggest that we are speaking at cross purposes due to
>different terminology. To my mind, the concept of a metaphor applies only one
>thing directly represents another.

It does, mostly. (Though be careful of confusing this with a metonym,
which is slightly different, involving making one aspect the whole.)

However, this is *representation*. One may talk about a spotlight as
being the sun. This does not make the spotlight *actually* the sun.
Metaphor often works on the level of similes in the background. That
is, whilst it is not presented as a simile textually, in substance it is
often effectively a simile, with undefined aspects. Rather than
something being specifically "as cool as a cucumber" - thus delineating
the aspects for comparison quite closely. A metaphor allows it to be
somewhat more open-ended, somewhat more subjective yet effectively an
undefined collection of similes.

>When an element is said to "represent" sex, I take this as meaning
>considerably more than saying that it can be related to sex or linked to sex,
>or that connections can be drawn to sex.

Connections can be drawn, and the trick is to work out how far those
connections can go.

On a purely image based level, working very crudely, comparison of a
vampiric bite to sex has various useful points of cross-over -
penetration, bodily fluids, potential rape overtones and so on.
Comparing it on many other aspects of sex will leave it purely blank.
One might mention pubic hair but it's wise to remember the Victorian
aspect of, hmm, how to put it, self-censorship. If you go through a lot
of fairy tales and so on as they were told at the time, there is a *lot*
of sexual imagery, veiled. One of the simple rules of thumb tends to be
that if it looks like a penis, it's a penis, a hole is a vagina and hair
is pubic hair. Obviously, these need to be tempered with common sense -
all too lacking in some slightly more forceful interpretations of a
work, attempting to twist *every* aspect to fit a theme. And remember
that Bram Stoker's Dracula has a moustache, IIRC, unlike many other
portrayals. An interesting aspect to consider, even if later discarded.

>>>OK. You are more than welcome, if you can, to explain how this particular
>>>theory improves one's understanding and appreciation of the story.
>>
>>Why would you have literary interpretation solely address the story
>>aspect? It can be far more enriching and rewarding than just that.
>>Indeed, a well-written piece of literature can be, indeed some might say
>>*should* be, about far more than simply the story.
>
>Once again, we are at semantic cross purposes. To me, the concept of a story
>encompasses everything in it.

There are many things *outside* a story of equally valid study.

One common theme 'recently' is to consider a piece of literature as a
free-standing entity, such that it grows and interacts. How you
interpret it and why, how it changes and how it grows, are just as valid
areas for thought and consideration.

>But rather than nitpick over words I would rather present a specific example
>from Dracula (which is both the first erotic passage and the first bloodsucking
>passage),

Exactly what I said. When working with direct practical criticism - as
this would be if slightly expanded with a few textual references as one
might do if given extracts from chapter three to examine critically - or
new criticism - which tends to end up as a sequence of themed mini-
practical criticisms - , it is possible to draw useful conclusions
regarding that passage as a free-standing entity. (A nod to its
existence within a whole work is, of course, more or less obligatory.)
In the whole novel, tracing sexual imagery in such a manner may draw far
more exciting and interesting conclusions than attempting to draw the
specific utility of them in any given situation - after all, even the
greatest of authors with a theme in hand (conscious, unconscious,
ironic, sarcastic, whatever) may lack something in the execution.
Comparing and contrasting an overview against the specifics may provide
far more illumination than taking one specific passage which supports
your view.

(Again, taking that one specific passage and arguing it to the hilt
would probably get you more research funding, however....)
